content: HIV is a chronic viral infection that can coexist with other infections, such as chronic hepatitis B (CHB). CHB is most commonly acquired during the perinatal period or early childhood and often precedes HIV infection in individuals who are co-infected. The prevalence of CHB among people living with HIV is similar to that observed in the general population. In regions with intermediate hepatitis B prevalence (2–8%, such as the Mediterranean, South America, and the Caribbean), transmission routes are mixed, and the prevalence of co-infection can vary. In the absence of treatment, HIV co-infection significantly alters the natural course of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. This includes faster progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), higher liver-related mortality, increased rates of chronic HBV infection after acute exposure, higher rates of HBV reactivation, and occult HBV infection (HBV DNA positivity without HBsAg positivity). Additionally, treatment response is reduced in co-infected individuals compared to those without HIV. Historically, co-infection management faced challenges such as cross-resistance between HIV and HBV drugs, increased liver injury due to direct hepatotoxicity or immune reconstitution hepatitis associated with antiretroviral therapy (ART), and the risk of fulminant hepatitis if ART did not adequately address both HIV and HBV. However, improved access to ART regimens active against HBV has significantly enhanced outcomes for co-infected individuals in recent years. People living with HIV are at a higher risk of acquiring hepatitis B. Therefore, all newly diagnosed HIV patients should be screened for HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HBc to identify those with CHB. Those who are not immune should be vaccinated, particularly individuals in high-risk groups such as people who inject drugs and men who have sex with men. However, the response to HBV vaccination is lower in people living with HIV, especially those with low CD4 cell counts. Studies have shown that a schedule of four double doses (40 µg) of the vaccine provides better protective anti-HBs titers than the standard three-dose schedule. Knowing the HBsAg status of people living with HIV is critical before initiating ART, switching regimens, or starting pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The recommended nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) drugs for ART regimens are tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC), as these are also active against HBV. WHO guidelines recommend TDF, entecavir (ETV), or TDF combined with FTC or 3TC for long-term treatment of CHB. All individuals co-infected with HIV and HBV should receive a TDF-based ART regimen combined with 3TC (or FTC) as the NRTI backbone, regardless of disease stage or HBV DNA levels. If ART drugs need to be changed due to HIV drug resistance or toxicity, TDF with 3TC or FTC should be continued alongside the new ART drugs. If TDF cannot be safely used, ETV is the recommended alternative for HBV therapy, provided it is combined with a fully suppressive ART regimen. Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) may be an option in specific clinical situations, such as concerns about renal or bone health, and for adolescents. Dolutegravir (DTG) combined with an NRTI backbone is the preferred first-line drug regimen for adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV, including those co-infected with HBV. Efavirenz (EFV) at a low dose (400 mg) is an alternative to DTG for adults and adolescents. HIV treatment regimens that do not include TDF may rarely lead to HBV flares due to ART-associated immune reconstitution. Similarly, abrupt discontinuation of TDF or 3TC can result in HBV reactivation, hepatic flares, and, in rare cases, hepatic decompensation. Long-term treatment strategies have achieved high rates of HBV DNA suppression (90%), HBeAg loss (46%), and HBsAg loss (12%) among HBeAg-positive individuals after five years of therapy, with no significant differences in response between those with and without HIV co-infection. To date, no definitive in vivo viral resistance to TDF has been described, although resistant strains have been identified. While the risk of developing cirrhosis is negligible for individuals co-infected with HBV and HIV receiving long-term tenofovir combined with FTC or 3TC, the risk of HCC persists, albeit at a lower level. Specialty care has been associated with higher-quality hepatitis B management for individuals with HBV and HIV co-infection, as well as those with HBV mono-infection. Leveraging HIV infrastructure, such as laboratory and pharmacy capacity, staff, and supply chains, offers an opportunity to expand care and treatment for people with HBV mono-infection and co-infection in lowand middle-income countries. Co-infection with hepatitis D virus (HDV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) is common in HBV-endemic regions. HCV co-infection is particularly prevalent among people who inject drugs, with up to 25% of those with HCV also having HBV. In many cases of co-infection, HCV is the dominant virus and may suppress HBV DNA levels. However, individuals with both HCV and HBV have a significantly higher risk of developing HCC, often presenting as a more aggressive and infiltrating form of cancer at a younger age. Treatment for both infections is generally required, with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) now forming the basis of therapy for HCV. Active or past HBV infection is not a contraindication to HCV therapy, but individuals starting HCV DAAs should be assessed for HBV infection and monitored for potential HBV reactivation. People co-infected with HBV and tuberculosis (TB) face unique challenges due to the overlapping endemic regions of these infections. Drug-induced liver injury is more common among individuals co-infected with HBV, HCV, or HIV who are receiving anti-TB drugs, necessitating careful monitoring. Similarly, people who inject drugs and prisoners are at high risk of acquiring HIV, HBV, HCV, and TB, and should be screened for all infections. Hepatitis B is also prevalent among individuals with end-stage renal disease, including kidney transplant recipients. These individuals should be screened for HBV, and seronegative individuals should be vaccinated. TDF and ETV require dose adjustments in those with renal impairment, and renal function should be monitored during antiviral therapy. In cases of acute hepatitis B, antiviral therapy is generally unnecessary for uncomplicated symptomatic cases, as most immunocompetent adults will spontaneously clear the infection. However, individuals with fulminant or severe acute hepatitis may benefit from nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy with ETV or TDF to improve survival and reduce the risk of recurrent hepatitis B.
